spread.heading: How it spreads
spread.intro: The same Aedes mosquitoes spread all three viruses, from person to mosquito to person.
spread.step1: A mosquito bites a person who has the virus.
spread.step2: The virus grows inside the mosquito.
spread.step3: The mosquito bites someone else and can pass the virus on.

listen.heading: Who we listen to
listen.lead: Outbite follows public health agencies first. Research comes in only to explain how well something works.

steps.title: CDC & EPA first
steps.text: U.S. health and environment agencies. Every tip is checked against their advice first, and all case numbers come from CDC.

steps.title: World Health Organization (WHO) to fill gaps
steps.text: When CDC and EPA don’t cover a topic, we use guidance from the World Health Organization.

steps.title: Research studies
steps.text: Published studies explain how well a step works, in “What the research says” on each tip.

rating.heading: How we label tips
rating.lead: Each tip has two separate labels: whether agencies recommend it, and how strong the research is.
rating.evidenceIntro: The badge always says what it measures, like “Strong: fewer bites”.

guidance.cdc-epa: Named in current CDC or EPA guidance.
guidance.who: Named in current WHO guidance, on a topic CDC and EPA don’t cover.
guidance.none: Based on research or a community program; agencies haven’t issued guidance.
guidance.unknown: Agencies say they don’t know if it works, like unregistered “natural” repellents.

evidence.moderate: Consistent evidence for a step along the way (fewer bites or mosquitoes), or one well-designed study on infection.
evidence.limited: Mixed results, or few and small studies.
evidence.emerging: A new method still being studied.
evidence.not-rated: The step comes from CDC or EPA guidance; Outbite hasn’t rated research for it.

numbers.heading: How the numbers update

dash.unitNote: Reported{ref} cases this year, including travel-related
dash.intro: Reported cases of dengue, Zika and chikungunya by state and territory, from CDC.
dash.meaning1: Most cases in U.S. states are in people who got sick while traveling.
dash.meaning2: A 0 doesn't mean there's no risk: protect your home anyway.
more: Reporting takes time. Health departments often add cases weeks later, so this year's numbers keep growing.
Weekly numbers are cases newly reported to CDC that week, not people who got sick that week. Reports can arrive weeks late, so many weeks show none.
These totals include people who were infected while traveling. CDC publishes the split between local and travel cases only for the whole country (shown below), not for each state here.
CDC counts each case where the person lives, not where they were bitten.
All numbers are early counts that can still change as more reports come in.
Many mild cases are never tested, so the real number is higher. Don't compare places or years directly.
